units.title: The Basic Path
units.desc: How a bill gets from an idea to the floor.

items.p: Put the usual steps for a bill in order, from introduction to the floor.
items.x: This is the textbook path, often called regular order. Many bills skip the hearing, and leadership sometimes skips committee entirely by bringing a bill straight to the floor.

items.p: Who can formally introduce a bill in the House?
o: Any member of the House
Any member, or the White House
Any registered lobbyist
Only committee chairs
items.x: Only members can introduce bills. Agencies, the White House and outside groups often write the text, but a member has to put it in. In the House that means dropping it in the “hopper,” a box on the floor.

items.p: Under the Constitution, which bills must start in the House?
o: Bills raising revenue
All bills over $1 billion
Treaties
Bills about elections
items.x: The Origination Clause (Article I, Section 7) requires revenue bills to start in the House, and by custom appropriations bills do too. The Senate works around this by taking a House-passed bill and replacing its text. The Affordable Care Act moved on H.R. 3590, which began as a tax bill about homeownership for service members.

items.p: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: The member who introduces the bill and leads on it
A member who formally signs on in support
A matching bill introduced in the other chamber
Sending a bill to the committee with jurisdiction
The box on the House floor where new bills are dropped
items.x: A long cosponsor list shows support, but it doesn’t move a bill. The committee does.

items.p: Who usually decides whether a bill gets a hearing or a markup?
o: The chair of the committee
The bill’s sponsor
The minority leader
The chamber’s parliamentarian
items.x: The chair controls the committee’s agenda. A bill the chair won’t schedule usually goes nowhere, whatever its cosponsor count.

items.p: In the House, who refers a new bill to committee?
o: The Speaker, advised by the parliamentarian
The bill’s sponsor, who names a committee when introducing it
The Rules Committee
The Clerk, who assigns new bills to committees by lottery
items.x: Referral is formally the Speaker’s call, made in practice on the parliamentarian’s advice about jurisdiction. A bill can go to several committees, and each one becomes a place where it can stall.

items.q: “The chair is going to mark up her own substitute.”
items.p: What does that tell you?
o: The committee will mark up the chair’s rewrite instead of the original
The bill is dead and won’t get a markup at all
The chair is leaving the committee and naming a substitute
The bill skips markup and goes straight to the floor
items.x: Committees often mark up an “amendment in the nature of a substitute,” which replaces the whole bill. The substitute is the text that matters from then on, so get a copy as soon as it circulates.

items.p: Roughly what share of introduced bills become law in a typical recent Congress?
o: A few percent
About a tenth
About a third
Most of them
items.x: Only a few percent of bills become law, and most never get a committee vote. Many are introduced to stake out a position, with no real plan to pass them.

units.title: The House Floor
units.desc: The majority controls the House floor, mostly through the Rules Committee.

items.p: What does a “rule” from the Rules Committee do?
o: Sets debate time and allowed amendments for one bill
Permanently changes the House’s standing rules for all future bills
Decides whether a bill is constitutional
Schedules committee hearings
items.x: Most major bills reach the House floor under a special rule written for that bill. The House has to adopt the rule by majority vote before it can debate the bill.

items.p: Match each type of rule to what it allows.
pairs: Any germane amendment can be offered
Only amendments the Rules Committee lists
Adopting the rule automatically changes the bill’s text
items.x: Open rules have become rare. Most major bills now come up under structured or closed rules, which lets the majority avoid amendment votes it doesn’t want.

items.p: Why is Rules called “the Speaker’s committee”?
o: The majority holds 9 of its 13 seats, and the Speaker picks them
The Speaker chairs it
It only meets when the Speaker attends
It writes the Speaker’s floor schedule
items.x: The 9 to 4 split and the Speaker’s control over majority appointments make Rules an arm of leadership. That control can slip: as part of his 2023 deal to become Speaker, Kevin McCarthy put hardliners on the committee who could block rules.

news.h: Majority members vote down their own party’s rule

items.p: What happens when a rule fails on the floor?
o: Leadership needs a new rule or another route to bring the bill up
The bill passes automatically without a separate vote
The Senate takes up its own version of the bill instead
The Speaker is removed and a new one must be elected
items.x: Rule votes used to be party-line formalities. Since 2023, hardliners in the majority have sunk rules to protest leadership, which can stall a bill even when it has the votes to pass.

items.p: Under “suspension of the rules,” what does a bill need to pass?
o: Two-thirds of those voting
A simple majority of those voting
60 votes
Unanimous consent
items.x: Most bills the House passes go through suspension, usually noncontroversial ones like naming post offices. It skips the Rules Committee entirely, at the cost of a two-thirds threshold.

news.h: Petition to force a vote on releasing the Epstein files gets its 218th signature

items.p: What does reaching 218 signatures do?
o: After a waiting period, it can force a vote over leadership’s objection
It passes the bill without a recorded floor vote
It sends the bill straight to the Senate, skipping a House vote
It removes the committee chair who blocked the bill
items.x: A discharge petition lets a majority of the House pull a bill out of committee. It rarely succeeds, because majority members don’t like to cross their own leaders. This one reached 218 when newly sworn-in Rep. Adelita Grijalva signed, after a delay in seating her that critics said was meant to stall the vote.

items.p: What is the motion to recommit?
o: The minority’s last chance to send a bill back to committee
A motion to restart the bill from scratch
A Senate motion to reconsider a vote that the chamber already took
A vote to override a veto
items.x: It comes right before the final vote and almost always fails. Since 2021, House rules have barred attaching amendment instructions to it, which used to make it the minority’s favorite tool for forcing awkward votes.

items.p: Put a major House bill’s floor steps in order.
items.x: If the rule fails at the second step, nothing after it happens.

units.title: The Senate Floor
units.desc: Unlimited debate means the Senate runs on agreement, and one senator can slow almost anything.

items.p: Why does the Senate do most of its business by unanimous consent?
o: Debate is nearly unlimited, so consent is much faster
The Constitution requires consent for most Senate business
Senate rules bar roll-call votes on routine matters
It makes votes easier to count
items.x: Consent agreements set when votes happen, which amendments get votes and how long debate lasts. Any one senator can object, which is where individual senators get their power.

items.p: A senator puts a hold on a nominee. What can the majority leader do?
o: Bring it to the floor anyway and file cloture
Nothing at all until the senator decides to lift it
Ask the parliamentarian to cancel the senator’s hold
Send the nomination to the House for its approval instead
items.x: A hold signals that the senator will object to fast-tracking. Leadership can get around it through cloture, but floor time is scarce, so holds on lower-priority items often work.

items.q: “We’ll have to file cloture on the motion to proceed first.”
items.p: What is the staffer telling you?
o: Even starting debate can be filibustered and needs 60 votes
The bill has passed
The bill is going to conference
The motion to proceed is just a formality before the real debate
items.x: The motion to start debating a bill is itself debatable. Opponents can force two cloture fights, one to begin debate and one to end it, and each one eats days of floor time.

items.p: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Skipping normal procedure by agreement; one objection blocks it
A senator’s warning they’ll object to moving something quickly
A roll call often used as a pause while senators negotiate
The motion to begin debate on a bill
Nonpartisan staff who advise on what the rules allow
items.x: When C-SPAN shows a quorum call, the real work is usually happening off the floor.

items.p: How many votes does cloture on a bill usually need?
o: 60, three-fifths of the Senate
67, two-thirds of the full Senate
50 plus the Vice President to break a tie
items.x: The rule is three-fifths of senators “duly chosen and sworn,” which is 60 when no seats are vacant. Ending debate on a change to the Senate’s rules takes two-thirds of those voting.

items.p: Does a senator have to keep talking on the floor to filibuster today?
o: No. Without 60 votes for cloture, it’s stuck
Yes, without stopping, or the bill moves to a vote
Yes, for at least 24 hours of continuous floor speeches
Only on bills, not nominations
items.x: The modern filibuster is the 60-vote threshold itself. Long speeches still happen, but they’re for attention and don’t decide the outcome.

items.p: Put the Senate’s cloture process for ending a filibuster in order.
items: A senator files a cloture motion
One full day of session passes
Up to 30 more hours of debate
items.x: Each cloture fight takes days. That time cost, as much as the 60 votes, is why leaders can only push a handful of contested bills through each year.

news.h: Senate Republicans change precedent to confirm nominees in batches

items.p: How could they change Senate practice with a simple majority?
o: They overruled the chair by majority vote
They passed a constitutional amendment allowing it
They found 67 votes to change the written rules
The parliamentarian signed off on the new practice
items.x: Changing the Senate’s written rules needs two-thirds to end debate, but a simple majority can set a new precedent by overruling the presiding officer. Democrats did this for most nominations in 2013, Republicans for Supreme Court nominees in 2017, and Republicans again in 2025 for batches of sub-Cabinet nominees. Cabinet and judicial nominees still go one at a time.

units.title: Money
units.desc: Spending runs on its own calendar and its own rules.

items.p: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: A law that creates or continues a program
A law that actually provides the money
Stopgap funding, usually at last year’s levels
Many appropriations bills combined into one
Funding a member directs to a specific project
items.x: Authorizers write the rules for a program. Appropriators decide how much it gets each year. An authorized program with no appropriation has no money.

items.p: How many regular appropriations bills does Congress write each year?
o: 12 bills
Just 1 bill
Only 4 bills
24 or more bills
items.x: There’s one for each pair of House and Senate appropriations subcommittees. Congress rarely passes all twelve on time, so it leans on continuing resolutions and omnibus packages.

news.h: Longest shutdown in U.S. history ends after 43 days

items.p: What causes a shutdown?
o: Appropriations lapse with no stopgap in place
The country hits the debt limit
The President vetoes the year’s budget resolution
The Senate rejects the President’s budget director
items.x: The fiscal year starts October 1. If neither the regular bills nor a continuing resolution is law by then, agencies without funding stop most work. Programs on mandatory spending, like Social Security payments, keep going.

items.p: Name a major kind of federal spending that isn’t funded through the annual appropriations bills.
o: Social Security benefits
The military
NASA’s space exploration programs
The FBI’s agents and field offices
items.x: Social Security, Medicare and most of Medicaid are “mandatory” spending, set by permanent law. Annual appropriations cover “discretionary” spending, roughly a quarter of the federal budget.

items.p: What makes reconciliation special in the Senate?
o: Debate is capped, so a simple majority can pass it
It needs no House vote
It doesn’t need the President’s signature to become law
It allows amendments without votes
items.x: Reconciliation is the main way a majority passes big tax and spending changes without 60 votes. The tradeoff is the Byrd rule, which limits it to provisions that are mainly budgetary.

items.p: Put the budget reconciliation process in order.
items: Congress adopts a budget resolution with reconciliation instructions
items.x: The budget resolution comes first because it unlocks the process. Without one, there’s no reconciliation bill.

items.p: Who advises on whether a provision violates the Byrd rule?
o: The Senate parliamentarian
The CBO director
The Chief Justice
The House Rules Committee
items.x: Staff run provisions past the parliamentarian in a process nicknamed the “Byrd bath.” A provision that fails can be struck unless 60 senators vote to waive the rule.

news.h: Senate passes the One Big Beautiful Bill Act 51-50, Vice President breaks the tie

items.p: Why could it pass with 51 votes instead of 60?
o: It moved through reconciliation
It was a proposed constitutional amendment
The minority agreed to skip cloture
It was a conference report
items.x: Final passage came after a vote-a-rama, the long series of amendment votes that follows once debate time runs out. Debate is capped, but senators can keep offering amendments, so these often run through the night.

units.title: Between the Chambers
units.desc: Nothing becomes law until both chambers pass the exact same text.

items.p: The House and Senate pass different versions of a bill. What has to happen?
o: Both chambers must pass identical text
The President picks which version becomes law
The longer version wins and goes to the President
The Senate’s version is final and goes to the President
items.x: The text has to match word for word. Differences get resolved by passing the bill back and forth with amendments, or through a conference committee.

items.p: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Chambers trade amendments until the text matches
Negotiators from both chambers write a compromise
The compromise text, voted up or down with no amendments
The official copy as passed by one chamber
The final version, passed by both and sent to the President
items.x: If you hear a bill is “enrolled,” Congress is done with it.

items.p: Why are formal conference committees rarer than they used to be?
o: In the Senate, setting one up takes several steps that can be filibustered
Both chambers voted to ban them in 2011 to speed up bills
The Constitution limits how often the two chambers can use them
The President must approve each one before it can meet
items.x: Leaders now usually work out the deal privately and move it through ping-pong. That puts the final text in a few hands, which matters if you’re trying to get a provision in.

items.p: What does that mean?
o: The Senate swaps its text into a House-passed bill
The bill will be left empty
The House will rewrite the Senate bill and send it back
They’ll wait for the next Congress and reintroduce the bill
items.x: Starting from a bill the House already passed saves a step and satisfies the rule that revenue bills start in the House. The original bill may have nothing to do with the final law.

items.p: What happens to bills that haven’t passed when a two-year Congress ends?
o: They die and must start over
They carry over automatically to the next Congress
They go to the President for a final decision
They become resolutions for the next Congress
items.x: Each Congress starts fresh. The 119th Congress ends January 3, 2027, so anything still pending then starts over in the 120th.

items.p: Why do so many unrelated provisions end up in the NDAA?
o: It’s must-pass and has become law every year for over 60 years
It can’t be amended once it reaches the floor
It skips the Senate and goes straight to the President
It’s exempt from committee review in both chambers
items.x: The annual defense authorization almost always becomes law, so members attach whatever they can get germane to it, including many AI and tech measures.

units.title: Endgame
units.desc: What the President can do, and what Congress can undo.

items.p: How long does the President have to act on a bill?
o: 10 days, not counting Sundays
30 days, not counting weekends or holidays
Until the current session of Congress ends
48 hours
items.x: If the President does nothing and Congress is in session, the bill becomes law without a signature after 10 days (Sundays excepted).

items.p: What is a pocket veto?
o: The bill dies unsigned because Congress adjourned
A veto the President announces privately, with no public message
A veto of one section of a bill, letting the rest become law
A veto issued before the bill has passed both chambers
items.x: A regular veto can be overridden. A pocket veto can’t, because Congress never gets the bill back to vote on. Which adjournments allow one has long been disputed between Congress and Presidents.

items.p: What does overriding a veto take?
o: Two-thirds of those voting in each chamber
60 in the Senate and a majority in the House
Three-fifths of each chamber
A majority plus the Vice President
items.x: Overrides are rare. Congress has overridden only about 7 percent of regular vetoes in its history.

items.p: Can the President veto just part of a bill?
o: No. The Supreme Court struck it down in 1998
Yes, for individual line items in spending bills
Yes, as long as a Senate majority consents to it
Yes, but Congress can restore the cut items by majority vote
items.x: In Clinton v. City of New York, the Court held that letting the President cancel parts of a signed law violated the Constitution’s process for making laws. A President who dislikes part of a bill has to veto all of it.

items.p: Put a fight over a presidential veto in order.
items: The President vetoes it and returns it with objections
The chamber where it started votes on override
The other chamber votes on override
items.x: The bill goes back to the chamber where it started. If that chamber fails to override, the other one never votes.

items.p: What does the Congressional Review Act let Congress do?
o: Overturn recent agency rules on a fast track
Rewrite any agency rule through a committee vote alone
Overturn federal court rulings on agency regulations
Fire the agency heads responsible for unpopular rules
items.x: The resolution still needs the President’s signature, so it mostly gets used right after a new President of the other party takes office, to undo the previous administration’s late rules.

items.p: A rule comes out in an outgoing administration’s final months. Why can the next Congress still overturn it?
o: The CRA’s lookback covers rules sent in about the last 60 session days before adjournment
New rules aren’t final until a full year after they’re published
Courts automatically send late rules back for the next administration
It can’t, because the rule is already final
items.x: That’s why rules finished in an administration’s last months are the most exposed, and why agencies race to finalize rules earlier in an election year.

items.p: After Congress overturns a rule under the CRA, what can the agency do?
o: It can’t issue a “substantially the same” rule unless Congress authorizes it
Reissue the same rule the next day under a new name
Appeal the resolution to the Supreme Court for review
Nothing changes, because the rule stays in effect exactly as written
items.x: This is sometimes called “salting the earth,” and it’s why CRA votes matter more than they look. Nobody is sure how different a new rule has to be.

items.p: Before 2017, how many times had the CRA been used successfully?
o: Once
Never
About 50
About a dozen times
items.x: It overturned a workplace ergonomics rule in 2001, and that was it until 2017 and 2018, when Congress used it to repeal 16 rules, most of them from the last months of the Obama administration. It has been used again after later transitions.

description: How a bill moves through Congress: committees, floor rules, the filibuster, money, vetoes and the Congressional Review Act.
